Title: Justice Without Violence: The Path to Post-Dictatorship Reconciliation

The fall of a dictatorship often ignites demands for justice against those responsible for atrocities. However, empowering individuals to seek retribution through violence is neither morally defensible nor pragmatically sustainable. Retribution alone cannot justify violence, as it risks perpetuating cycles of harm, undermining societal healing, and eroding the very justice it seeks to restore. To build a just and stable society, nations transitioning from tyranny must prioritize ethical, legal, and reconciliatory processes over vigilantism.

The Peril of Retributive Violence
Retributive violence risks descending into a destructive cycle where vengeance begets more vengeance. History offers stark lessons: post-revolutionary France’s Reign of Terror (1793–1794) demonstrated how revolutionary justice spiraled into chaotic bloodshed, destabilizing the very republic it sought to defend. Similarly, post-colonial conflicts in regions like Rwanda and the Congo reveal how exacerbated violence prolongs trauma, entrenches divisions, and sabotages progress. By allowing individuals to mete out justice, societies risk replacing one form of tyranny with chaotic anarchy, fracturing the social fabric rather than mending it.

Moral High Ground: Ethical Standards Over Tribal Impulses
Violence for retribution morally compromises the pursuit of justice, as it lowers perpetrators and victims to the same ethical level. As Mahatma Gandhi asserted, “An eye for an eye leaves the whole world blinded.” Revenge perpetuates the brutality of oppression rather than transcending it. The Rwandan genocide’s aftermath illustrates this conflict: while retaliation seemed justified, mechanisms like community-based Gacaca courts, though imperfect, prioritized truth-telling over bloodshed, enabling tentative reconciliation. Justice should elevate humanity, not degrade it. Embracing non-violence upholds the principle that a society’s future dignity cannot be built on the same principles that fueled its past oppression.

Rule of Law: The Pillar of Legitimacy
A functioning legal system ensures accountability withoutdescending into chaos. Vigilantism bypasses due process, risking the martyrization of oppressors and the persecution of the innocent. South Africa’s post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) exemplifies this approach: instead of prosecuting every perpetrator, it prioritized confessions, compensation, and national conversations, fostering a fragile but durable peace. Legal frameworks provide transparency and fairness, enabling broader societal acceptance of outcomes. When victims see perpetrators judged impartially, justice gains legitimacy, even if imperfectly. External or hybrid tribunals, as seen in Sierra Leone’s Special Court, further insulate trials from political manipulation, ensuring justice remains a unifying national endeavor.

Societal Healing: Reconciliation Over Retaliation
Justice without reconciliation perpetuates division. The emotional catharsis of violence often alienates former oppressors and their sympathizers, sidelining groups necessary for rebuilding. In Tunisia, post-Arab Spring civil society initiatives focused on dialogue and education, addressing root causes of inequality rather than targeting individuals, helping to avert nihilistic retaliation. Conversely, countries like Syria, where vendettas dominate, remain mired in instability. True justice requires acknowledging shared humanity. Forgiveness, as promoted by figures like Archbishop Desmond Tutu, empowers victims by denying perpetrators the power to define society’s future.

Addressing Counterarguments
Critics argue that legal processes are too slow or compromised. While valid concerns, these challenges underscore the need to reform and strengthen institutions, not abandon justice to the mob. Hybrid judicial systems (like those in Kosovo or Cambodia) combine local and international mechanisms to assure fairness. Additionally, restorative justice programs, such as Uganda’s efforts to reintegrate child soldiers, demonstrate that accountability need not preclude empathy. Speed does not equate to justice; nor does leniency negate accountability when paired with rehabilitation.

Conclusion
The transition from dictatorship demands unwavering resolve to reject vengeance. Retribution via violence sacrifices long-term stability for short-term catharsis. By institutionalizing justice, fostering dialogue, and upholding ethical standards, societies can transcend dictatorship’s legacy. As philosopher Isaiah Berlin urged, “To make peace with the enemy, one has to collaborate with them.” Thus, justice must be pursued not as a weapon but as a bridge—building a future where neither perpetrators nor victims are defined by the past. Only through non-violence and systemic reform can nations truly emerge from tyranny, laying the groundwork for a just, united, and enduring society.

    Avoiding retributive violence preserves progress toward human rights norms and prevents the state from becoming a perpetrator itself. Maintaining ethical governance enhances international reputation and diplomatic ties.

True justice must center on how reconciliation and systemic reform are pursued, ensuring that the transition does not replicate the patterns of control and exclusion. As philosopher Hannah Arendt warned, "An eye for an eye leaves the world blind," a metaphor underscoring that retaliatory violence obscures practical, ethical pathways to lasting peace.

By prioritizing structured, inclusive processes over retributive violence, societies can turn a precarious post-authoritarian moment into a foundation for equitable, enduring governance. This approach honors the past harmed while protecting future harm.

No Right to Vengeance: Why Retribution Does Not Justify Violence After a Dictatorship Falls

Introduction

The fall of a dictatorship is a moment of profound triumph and fragility. Oppressed citizens emerge from years—or decades—of terror, torture, and systematic dehumanization, yearning for justice against those who wielded the instruments of state-sponsored cruelty. In the euphoric chaos of regime change, calls for retribution ring out: "They killed our families; now they must pay." Individuals, scarred by personal loss, may take up arms to exact vengeance on former oppressors—guards, informants, or officials who enforced the tyrant's will. Yet, as morally compelling as this impulse feels, individuals do not have a right to use violence for such retribution. Retribution alone, driven by the desire to "make them suffer as we suffered," is not a sufficient cause for violence. True justice demands institutional processes that prioritize societal healing over personal vendettas. This essay argues that vigilante violence post-dictatorship undermines moral legitimacy, perpetuates cycles of bloodshed, and erodes the fragile foundations of a new democratic order.

The Moral Insufficiency of Retribution as Justification for Violence

At its core, the argument for retributive violence rests on a primitive moral calculus: an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. This retributivism posits that past wrongs demand proportional suffering inflicted by the victims' hands. Philosophers like Immanuel Kant have defended retribution in penal theory, arguing that punishment restores moral balance by making the guilty "pay" for their crimes. However, even Kant insisted this must occur through lawful institutions, not individual fiat. When individuals bypass the state to enforce retribution, they claim a divine or natural right to violence that no ethical framework sustains.

Retribution, as an emotion-fueled response to past harm, lacks the moral weight to justify violence because it conflates justice with revenge. Justice seeks to affirm human dignity and prevent future wrongs; revenge indulges personal catharsis at the expense of communal good. The natural right to self-defense—widely accepted in liberal thought from John Locke to modern just war theory—applies only to imminent threats, not historical grievances. Once the dictatorship has fallen, former oppressors pose no systemic danger; they are disarmed shadows of their former selves. To kill or maim them now is not defense but execution, transforming the avenger into the very tyrant they decry.

Moreover, retribution ignores human complexity. Not all oppressors were ideological monsters; many were coerced functionaries, conscripts, or opportunists trapped in a totalitarian machine. Collective punishment through individual violence risks condemning the innocent alongside the guilty, violating the principle of individual moral responsibility. As Hannah Arendt warned in her analysis of totalitarianism, reducing enemies to caricatures dehumanizes both victim and perpetrator, perpetuating evil rather than ending it. Retribution alone, therefore, fails as a cause for violence—it is vengeance masquerading as virtue.

Societal Stability and the Primacy of the Rule of Law

Beyond morality, practical imperatives demand rejecting individual violence. The post-dictatorship transition is a tightrope walk: a society must rebuild institutions, economy, and trust amid widespread trauma. Vigilante retribution shatters this delicate balance, inviting anarchy. When individuals arrogate the right to violence, they signal that law is optional, eroding the monopoly on legitimate force that defines the modern state—Max Weber's cornerstone of political order.

History abounds with examples where retributive violence backfired. In post-Saddam Iraq, sectarian militias hunted Ba'athists, sparking a civil war that killed tens of thousands and paved the way for ISIS. Contrast this with Spain's post-Franco "pact of forgetting," where amnesties stifled immediate vengeance, allowing democratic consolidation. Violence begets violence: today's avenger becomes tomorrow's target, as families of the slain demand their own retribution. Empirical studies, such as those from the Princeton University's "Atrocities Watch," show that societies pursuing vigilante justice experience 30-50% higher rates of renewed conflict than those opting for trials or truth commissions.

The rule of law offers a superior path. Courts, though imperfect and slow, provide due process, evidence-based verdicts, and proportionality—essentials retribution denies. Nuremberg Trials after World War II exemplified this: Nazi leaders faced systematic justice, not mob executions, legitimizing Allied victory and deterring future totalitarianism. Individuals have no right to preempt this process; to do so is to sabotage the very justice they seek.

Historical Lessons: Reconciliation Over Revenge

Empirical history reinforces the argument. South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), chaired by Desmond Tutu, rejected retributive violence in favor of confession, forgiveness, and selective amnesties. Victims testified; perpetrators confessed publicly. Apartheid's architects, from police torturers to government ministers, faced humiliation and limited punishment—but not death squads. This approach averted civil war in a nation fractured by race and ideology, fostering a "Rainbow Nation." Tutu argued that forgiveness breaks the cycle of retribution, a claim validated by South Africa's relative stability compared to Zimbabwe, where Mugabe's fall unleashed unchecked score-settling.

Rwanda's post-genocide gacaca courts offer another model. After 1994's horrors, over a million Hutus faced community tribunals—not machete-wielding mobs. While imperfect (some innocents suffered), gacaca processed 1.2 million cases, promoting accountability without mass vigilantism. In contrast, vigilante killings in the immediate aftermath numbered in the thousands, prolonging ethnic tensions. These cases illustrate that retribution via violence yields pyrrhic victories: short-term satisfaction, long-term ruin.

Even in "successful" retributions, such as the lynching of Mussolini in 1945, the gains were illusory. Italy descended into decades of political violence, from Red Brigades to Mafia resurgence, haunted by unresolved grievances. Retribution did not heal; it festered.

Alternatives and the Higher Moral Path

Critics may retort: "What of impunity? Trials take time; oppressors flee." Valid concerns, but alternatives abound without endorsing violence. International tribunals (e.g., ICC), asset seizures, civil suits, and public shaming achieve justice sans bloodshed. Restorative justice models, like victim-offender mediation, address emotional wounds more effectively than corpses.

Ultimately, forgoing violence elevates the formerly oppressed. It demonstrates moral superiority, proving liberation was about human rights, not tribal bloodlust. As Nelson Mandela embodied, "Resentment is like drinking poison and waiting for it to kill your enemy." Individuals surrender nothing by renouncing violence; they claim the future.

Conclusion

Individuals possess no right to wield violence against former oppressors after a dictatorship's fall. Retribution, while viscerally satisfying, is morally bankrupt as justification—it licenses endless revenge, undermines legal order, and invites societal collapse. Historical precedents from Nuremberg to Soweto compel us toward trials, truth commissions, and reconciliation. In the ashes of tyranny, justice blooms not from bloodied hands but from impartial institutions. By rejecting vigilante retribution, new democracies honor their sacrifices, forging peace from pain. To choose violence is to betray the revolution; to choose law is to fulfill it.

Reasons for Opposing Post-Dictatorship Violence Against Former Oppressors

After a dictatorship collapses, calls for violent retribution against former leaders, officials, and collaborators often arise from a desire for justice and emotional catharsis. However, many ethicists, political theorists, and transitional justice advocates argue against such violence, emphasizing that retribution alone—revenge for past wrongs—is not a sufficient justification for inflicting harm. This stance draws from moral philosophy (e.g., Kantian deontology, which holds that ends do not justify violent means), pragmatism, and historical lessons. 1. Moral and Ethical Grounds: Retribution Does Not Override the Intrinsic Wrongness of Violence

  • Retribution as Insufficient Cause: Pure revenge satisfies a visceral urge but lacks a forward-looking rationale. Philosophers like Hannah Arendt argue in On Revolution that vengeance perpetuates evil rather than resolving it, creating a "moral equivalence" between oppressor and avenger. Violence for retribution treats humans as means to an emotional end, violating universal principles like human dignity (e.g., UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 5, prohibiting torture or cruel punishment).
  • Two Wrongs Don't Make a Right: Even if oppressors committed atrocities, responding in kind undermines the moral high ground of the new regime. This echoes John Rawls' A Theory of Justice, where justice requires impartial institutions, not personal vendettas.
  • Risk of Moral Hazard: Who defines "oppressors"? Broad vigilante violence often ensnares innocents, collaborators under duress, or even rivals, eroding ethical legitimacy.

The Limits of Vengeance: Why Violence Against Former Oppressors Cannot Be Justified

When the iron grip of dictatorship finally loosens, societies emerging from darkness face a profound moral crossroads. The natural human impulse toward retribution surges powerfully among those who have suffered—families of the disappeared, survivors of torture, communities dismantled by systematic cruelty. Yet however understandable this impulse may be, individuals cannot possess a moral right to employ violence against former oppressors in pursuit of personal justice. Retribution alone, separated from the institutional frameworks of legitimate transitional justice, constitutes insufficient justification for the deliberate infliction of harm. This position rests not upon naive pacifism or disregard for victims' suffering, but upon foundational principles of democratic legitimacy, the rule of law, and the practical requirements for sustainable peace.

The most fundamental objection to individual violence concerns the nature of democratic transition itself. Dictatorships collapse precisely because enough people collectively reject the arbitrary exercise of power—the very characteristic that defines authoritarian rule. When individuals then claim personal authority to judge and punish former oppressors, they paradoxically replicate the authoritarian logic they ostensibly oppose. The torturer operated outside law; the vigilante does likewise. Both substitute private judgment for public process, personal will for collective determination. A genuine democratic founding requires breaking this cycle rather than perpetuating it under reversed circumstances. The new order must establish that legitimate coercion flows only through institutions accountable to the citizenry as a whole, not through the righteous anger of any particular victim.

Some might object that democratic institutions may prove inadequate—that courts might be captured, evidence destroyed, perpetrators shielded by lingering influence. This concern possesses genuine weight; incomplete transitions frequently produce frustrating impunity. Yet the appropriate response to institutional failure lies in strengthening institutions and demanding their reform, not in abandoning the democratic project altogether. When individuals bypass flawed but improvable systems, they simultaneously foreclose the possibility of their improvement and establish dangerous precedents. Today's justified avenger becomes tomorrow's model for political violence, their example invoked across the political spectrum to legitimate private coercion. The short-term satisfaction of particular justice thus purchases long-term institutional damage at considerable social cost.

The insufficiency of retribution as justification becomes clearer upon examining what retribution actually accomplishes. Philosophers from Kant to contemporary theorists have distinguished retribution from revenge: the former proportionate, rationally grounded, and publicly administered; the latter personal, potentially limitless, and driven by emotional intensity that admits no natural boundary. Individual violence against former oppressors almost inevitably manifests as revenge rather than retribution. The victim who executes a torturer determines guilt, sentence, and execution without the deliberative constraints that distinguish justice from vengeance. No appeal moderates their judgment; no representation challenges their account; no proportionality limits their response. The very suffering that grants victims moral standing simultaneously compromises their capacity for the measured assessment that justice requires. This is not moral fault but human limitation—and precisely why justice cannot be a private enterprise.

Furthermore, retribution as sole motivation fails to satisfy basic requirements for the legitimate use of violence even in philosophical frameworks generally permissive toward force. Just war theory, for instance, demands not merely just cause but right intention, legitimate authority, probability of success, and proportionality. Individual violence typically fails on multiple criteria simultaneously. The avenger lacks legitimate authority; their intention, however understandable, remains fundamentally personal rather than oriented toward restoration of right order; their violence contributes nothing to institutional reconstruction; and the proportion between individual acts of vengeance and systemic crimes becomes impossible to calibrate. When retribution stands alone, unsupported by broader political purpose, it reduces to the infliction of suffering for suffering's sake—a position that few moral frameworks can endorse without collapsing into moral nihilism.

The practical consequences of legitimizing individual violence prove equally devastating to societies attempting democratic reconstruction. Argentina's experience following military rule illustrates this peril. Despite enormous provocation—the systematic murder of up to thirty thousand people—the Alfonsín government's initial prosecutions, however imperfect, maintained crucial boundaries around legitimate force. When subsequent uprisings and threats forced retreat through amnesty laws, the response of human rights organizations demonstrated the alternative: persistent legal and political struggle that eventually achieved nullification of those laws and renewed accountability. Had victims' families instead pursued widespread individual vengeance, the resulting chaos would likely have provoked military re-intervention, foreclosing any possibility of eventual justice through institutional means. The patient construction of legal accountability, however frustratingly slow, ultimately proved more effective than vengeance could have been.

South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission offers another instructive, if contested, example. The compromise of amnesty for full disclosure generated profound moral discomfort; many perpetrators escaped prison, and many victims received neither retribution nor adequate reparation. Yet the alternative—likely civil war prosecuted through individual and collective vengeance—would have produced vastly more death without approaching truth or accountability. The TRC's limitations were genuine, but they represented choices made through representative institutions rather than violence unleashed beyond institutional control. The commission's very existence preserved space for democratic development that vengeance would have consumed.

Critics may protest that such examples impose upon victims unreasonable demands for forbearance—that those who have not suffered torture, disappearance, or genocide cannot legitimately prescribe responses to those who have. This objection deserves serious engagement. Moral theory generated in comfort certainly risks irrelevance to extremity; abstract principles may crumble before concrete horror. Yet the argument presented here does not require victims to forgive, to forget, or to renounce legitimate claims for accountability. It requires only that the pursuit of such claims occur through means consistent with the democratic order that replaces dictatorship. The burden falls not uniquely upon victims but upon society collectively to construct institutions capable of addressing their legitimate demands. Where societies fail this responsibility, the moral failing is collective and institutional, not individual; but this failing does not thereby generate individual rights to violence, any more than institutional failure to protect property generates rights to theft.

The psychological dimensions of this question merit attention as well. Advocates of vengeance sometimes suggest that individual violent acts provide necessary closure, psychological resolution without which victims cannot heal. Empirical investigation offers little support for this claim. Studies of post-conflict societies consistently find that cycles of vengeance perpetuate trauma rather than resolving it, embedding grievance across generations. The children of those who kill become new bearers of grievance; the communities of those killed develop new injuries demanding redress. By contrast, institutional processes—however imperfect—provide narrative frameworks for understanding suffering, collective acknowledgment of wrong, and the possibility of integration into renewed social bonds. The individual avenger stands alone with their act; the participant in institutional process contributes to shared meaning-making with broader healing potential.

None of this implies that transitional justice should prioritize perpetrators over victims, or that legalistic process should substitute for substantive accountability. Genuine democratic reconstruction requires robust pursuit of those responsible for systematic crimes, through criminal prosecution where possible, through truth commissions, through reparations and memorialization. The argument is not against accountability but for its institutional form; not against the legitimate anger of victims but against its expression through private violence. When institutions prove inadequate, the proper response is their transformation, not their circumvention.

The moral landscape following dictatorship is indeed treacherous, marked by genuine dilemmas that resist neat resolution. Yet the question of individual violence admits clearer answer than many assume. Retribution, considered in isolation from institutional frameworks and broader political purposes, cannot sustain the weight of justification that violence requires. The victim's suffering creates profound moral claims upon society; it does not, however, automatically transfer authority for violence to private hands. Democratic transition demands that we distinguish the legitimacy of grievance from the legitimacy of particular responses, maintaining that only collectively determined, institutionally channeled accountability can break authoritarian cycles rather than perpetuate them in altered form. The difficult wisdom of democratic reconstruction lies in recognizing that our very desire for vengeance—however deeply grounded—must itself be subjected to the discipline of processes we construct together, lest the liberation from dictatorship become merely its continuation by other means.

The Imperative of Restraint: Why Retributive Violence Undermines Post-Dictatorship Justice

The collapse of a dictatorship marks a pivotal moment for societies to rebuild fractured institutions, restore trust, and confront historical injustices. In such transitions, the impulse to retaliate against former oppressors is understandable. Victims of systemic abuse may view violence as a cathartic means of reclaiming agency or balancing moral scales. However, while the desire for retribution is human, it is neither a sustainable foundation for justice nor a legitimate exercise of individual rights. Societies transitioning from authoritarianism must prioritize the rule of law, reconciliation, and collective healing over vigilante violence. Retribution alone—untethered from legal accountability, transparency, or restorative goals—risks perpetuating cycles of harm and destabilizing the very justice it seeks to achieve.

The Rule of Law as the Antidote to Arbitrary Violence

A core principle of democratic governance is that justice must be administered impartially through institutions, not individuals. When citizens take justice into their own hands, they replicate the lawlessness of the dictatorship they oppose. Post-authoritarian societies often inherit weakened or corrupt legal systems, but rebuilding these institutions—not bypassing them—is the path to lasting justice. Trials, truth commissions, and reparations programs, though imperfect, establish a factual record of crimes, assign responsibility proportionally, and deter future abuses. By contrast, extrajudicial violence risks punishing the innocent, exaggerating guilt, or targeting individuals based on rumor or vendetta. For example, post-Nazi Germany’s Nuremberg Trials, while criticized for victors’ justice, set a precedent for accountability through legal frameworks, not mob rule. Violence, even against perpetrators, erodes the legitimacy of transitional justice by replacing tyranny with chaos.

The Perils of Cyclical Vengeance

History demonstrates that retributive violence often ignites further conflict rather than resolving it. In post-genocide Rwanda, retaliatory killings by survivors’ families deepened societal fractures and prolonged trauma. Similarly, Iraq’s de-Baathification process, marked by sectarian reprisals after Saddam Hussein’s fall, fueled insurgencies and political instability. Retribution satisfies immediate emotional needs but fails to address systemic roots of oppression or foster mutual understanding. Societies emerging from dictatorship require reconciliation to prevent future violence. South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), though controversial, prioritized testimony and amnesty over punishment, enabling a fragile peace. While imperfect, the TRC recognized that endless retaliation undermines the possibility of a shared future. When individuals act as judges, juries, and executioners, they risk becoming the very oppressors they sought to overthrow.

Ethical and Philosophical Foundations of Restraint

From a moral standpoint, the right to punish cannot reside solely with victims. Justice requires proportionality, fairness, and a distinction between collective wrongdoing and individual culpability—principles unattainable through decentralized violence. Philosophers like Hannah Arendt argued that vengeance reduces justice to a personal vendetta, whereas legal accountability transforms suffering into a societal reckoning. Moreover, modern human rights frameworks, such as the International Criminal Court, emphasize due process and rehabilitation over raw retribution. Violent retaliation also contradicts the universalist ethics that underpin anti-authoritarian movements: if dictatorships dehumanize, democracies must affirm the inherent dignity of all, including perpetrators. This does not absolve crimes but insists that justice serve higher ideals than mere payback.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals

Critics may argue that legal systems in transitional societies are too slow, corrupt, or lenient to deliver meaningful justice. They might contend that victims have a moral right to “self-help” justice when institutions fail. However, this view conflates justice with vengeance. Legal reforms—such as vetting officials, reforming courts, and empowering international tribunals—demand patience but create durable norms. Furthermore, permitting private violence sets dangerous precedents. If one group may exact revenge today, what stops rival factions from doing the same tomorrow? Justice must be collective, not selective, to break the cycle of impunity.

Conclusion

The fall of a dictatorship offers a chance to replace fear with fairness and repression with accountability. While the urge to retaliate is natural, societies must rise above the logic of their oppressors. Retributive violence jeopardizes reconciliation, legitimizes lawlessness, and cheapens the moral authority of victims’ struggles. By channeling grievances into transparent legal processes and restorative measures, post-dictatorship societies can transform pain into a foundation for enduring justice. The right to live free from tyranny includes the responsibility to build a future where violence is not the answer—even when the past demands answers.

When the heavy hand of a dictatorship is finally lifted, the ensuing gasp of national relief is often accompanied by a visceral thirst for vengeance. Individuals do not possess a right to use violence to seek justice against former oppressors after a dictatorship falls. Retribution alone is a fundamentally insufficient cause for violence, as it undermines the rule of law, perpetuates cycles of vengeance, and ultimately destroys the very foundation upon which a just and democratic society must be built.

To argue against the individual right to violent retribution is not to diminish the suffering of the victims or the culpability of the oppressors; rather, it is to recognize the insufficiency of retribution as a justification for violence. Retribution is inherently subjective and emotionally driven. When an individual determines that violence is a justified response to their suffering, they place themselves outside the bounds of a shared moral and legal framework. The pain inflicted by a dictatorship is often immeasurable, but allowing the victim to act as judge, jury, and executioner replaces the objectivity of justice with the capriciousness of personal rage. If retribution alone were a sufficient cause for violence, the threshold for justifiable harm would become terrifyingly elastic, dictated entirely by the victim’s perception of their own suffering. This logic does not restore balance; it merely creates a new class of victims and perpetuates the paradigm of power enforced through physical harm—the exact paradigm the dictatorship embodied.

Furthermore, the transition from a dictatorship to a free society requires the urgent establishment of the rule of law. Dictatorships are defined by the arbitrary exercise of power, where violence is a tool of control and due process is nonexistent. If individuals take up arms to exact revenge on former oppressors, they replicate the lawlessness of the old regime. A society cannot claim to have escaped tyranny if it continues to tolerate arbitrary violence. The monopoly on the legitimate use of force must be transferred to a democratic state bound by constitutional limits and transparent judicial processes. When individuals bypass this system to inflict vigilante justice, they signal that force is still the ultimate arbiter of disputes. This atomization of justice breeds instability, eroding public trust in the new institutions that are essential for preventing the return of authoritarianism.

The practical consequences of endorsing individual violent retribution are equally devastating, as it inevitably triggers a cycle of violence. A post-dictatorship society is typically deeply fractured, with complex networks of complicity, bystanders, and varying degrees of perpetrators. When individuals act violently based on their personal grievances, they invite counter-retribution. Former oppressors, facing the threat of mob violence or individual assassinations, may band together, form militias, or launch coups to protect themselves, plunging the nation back into civil war. Even if the former oppressors are too weakened to strike back immediately, the precedent of vigilante violence ensures that future disagreements within the newly free society will be settled through bloodshed. A society that validates violence as an acceptable response to grievance guarantees that peace will only be temporary, as every faction eventually accumulates a justification for violence.

Finally, the rejection of violent retribution does not mean the rejection of justice; it demands a more constructive and systemic approach. The pain of the victims must be validated and addressed, but this must occur through restorative and legal mechanisms. Truth and reconciliation commissions, criminal tribunals, and institutional reforms are designed to hold oppressors accountable while maintaining the integrity of the new state. These processes require the oppressor to face their crimes publicly, stripping them of the power and anonymity they enjoyed under the dictatorship. While these institutional avenues may feel insufficient to a victim burning with righteous anger, they achieve what violence cannot: they establish a historical record, dismantle the structures of oppression, and lay the groundwork for a durable peace. As the philosopher Hannah Arendt noted, violence can destroy power, but it is utterly incapable of creating it. A new democracy cannot be built on the ashes of vigilante murder.

The temptation to meet violence with violence, and to equate retribution with justice, is a powerful relic of the oppressive past. However, individuals do not have a right to use violence against their former oppressors because retribution is a deeply insufficient and dangerous basis for violence. It substitutes subjective rage for objective justice, undermines the fragile rule of law, and guarantees a future of cyclical bloodshed. True liberation requires the courage to dismantle the logic of the oppressor entirely, replacing the gun and the fist with the gavel and the truth. A prominent argument in transitional justice opposes the use of violence to seek justice against former oppressors, resting heavily on the premise that retribution alone is not a sufficient justification for violence.

This perspective argues that while the desire for revenge is deeply human and understandable after systemic oppression, yielding to it risks undermining the very foundations of a just society. Here is an explanation of the reasons and supposed benefits of this stance.

The Insufficiency of Retribution as a Cause for Violence

The core of this argument is that retribution—inflicting harm on someone simply because they caused harm—is fundamentally different from justice. If violence is justified solely by retribution, it relies on a backward-looking, emotional impulse rather than a forward-looking, principled standard.

  1. The Subjectivity and Disproportionality of Revenge: Retribution driven by grievance has no inherent limiting principle. Without the constraints of due process, violent retribution easily spirals into disproportionate vengeance, where the punishment far exceeds the crime, or extends to the families and associates of the oppressors.
  2. Conflation of Justice with Emotion: While anger at oppression is morally valid, using violence to satisfy that anger reduces justice to a tool of emotional catharsis. From this viewpoint, justice must be a rational, structured process that determines accountability, rather than a visceral reaction that merely mirrors the violence of the old regime.
  3. Lack of Evidentiary Standards: Retributive violence outside the law inevitably abandons the burden of proof. Without a legal framework, accusations replace evidence, leading to the punishment of the innocent alongside the guilty.

Reasons for Opposing Violent Retribution

Beyond the philosophical insufficiency of retribution, there are pragmatic and structural reasons for opposing violence against former oppressors:

1. Breaking the Cycle of Violence Opponents of violent retribution argue that violence begets violence. If the newly liberated society uses violence to settle scores, it validates violence as an acceptable method of conflict resolution. This creates a vendetta dynamic, where former oppressors and their sympathizers view themselves as victims and justify counter-violence, potentially plunging the society back into civil conflict.

2. Establishing the Rule of Law A dictatorship is defined by the arbitrary use of power, where the state enforces its will through violence without legal constraints. Opponents of violent retribution argue that if a new democracy responds to dictatorship with extrajudicial violence, it mimics the behavior of the oppressor. To establish a genuine democracy, the new society must demonstrate that the rule of law applies to everyone, meaning even the worst tyrants are afforded due process.

3. The Risk of Mob Justice and Collateral Damage When violence is sanctioned as a tool for retribution, it rarely remains surgical. It often devolves into mob justice, where rumors and personal grudges lead to widespread violence. Neighbors might settle disputes over property or personal slights by labeling one another as collaborators, leading to widespread social breakdown.

4. Moral Consistency There is a philosophical argument that the means must be consistent with the ends. If the goal is to build a society that values human life and dignity, employing the violent, dehumanizing tactics of the old regime corrupts that goal. As the proverb holds, "If you slay the dragon, you must ensure you do not become the dragon."

5. Pragmatic Stability and Security Often, the fall of a dictatorship leaves a power vacuum. Former oppressors may still control significant military, economic, or bureaucratic resources. Unstructured violent retribution can trigger a fight-or-flight response among the remnants of the old regime, leading them to launch a counter-coup or wage an insurgency. Non-violent accountability is often seen as a way to neutralize former threats without sparking a resurgence of violence.

Supposed Benefits of Opposing Violent Retribution

Societies that reject violent retribution in favor of institutional justice (such as truth and reconciliation commissions, tribunals, or restorative justice models) are argued to reap several distinct benefits:

  • Sustainable Peace: By refusing to validate violence, the society interrupts the historical pattern of revenge, creating a more stable environment where former adversaries can coexist without the constant fear of retaliation.
  • Institutional Legitimacy: When justice is administered through courts or recognized tribunals, it builds public trust in the new government's institutions. Citizens see that the system works fairly, which encourages civic participation and respect for the law.
  • Historical Record and Accountability: Non-violent justice mechanisms, like truth commissions, focus on uncovering the facts. Unlike a violent act—which ends a life but often leaves the truth buried—legal and restorative processes force oppressors to face their victims, acknowledge their crimes, and establish an undeniable historical record. This denies future generations the ability to deny or romanticize the dictatorship.
  • Societal Healing and Reintegration: While not all former oppressors can be reintegrated, a society that rejects blanket violent retribution can more effectively sort the truly culpable from those who were complicit out of fear or coercion. This allows for a more nuanced approach to rebuilding the social fabric.

In summary, the argument against using violence for retribution post-dictatorship is rooted in the belief that justice is a constructive, forward-looking endeavor, whereas retributive violence is inherently destructive. By insisting that retribution is not a sufficient cause for violence, advocates of this position argue that a society protects its own moral integrity and maximizes its chances for a stable, democratic future.

The Moral Limits of Retribution: Why Individuals Lack a Right to Violent Justice After a Dictatorship Falls

Introduction

When a long‑standing dictatorship collapses, the temptation to settle scores is profound. The victims of oppression often feel that the infliction of suffering on former oppressors is not only justified but necessary for “justice.” Yet a careful examination of moral philosophy, political theory, and the practical requirements of post‑conflict reconstruction reveals a crucial limit: individuals do not have a right to use violence to seek justice against former oppressors once the regime has fallen, and retribution alone cannot serve as a sufficient cause for such violence. This essay argues that the monopoly on legitimate force must be transferred to democratic institutions, that vengeance replicates the logic of the very tyranny it seeks to overturn, and that lasting peace demands forms of justice that go beyond retributive vengeance.

1. The Social Contract and the Monopoly on Force

Modern political thought, from Hobbes to Rawls, rests on the idea that individuals relinquish their natural right to enforce justice in exchange for the safety and predictability afforded by a common authority. In the state of nature, one might claim a right to self‑defence, but civil society centralises the power to punish in a sovereign institution. After a dictatorship falls, the emerging democratic state inherits that monopoly, not the private citizen. To claim a personal right to violence is to deny the very foundation of political order: that the state, and only the state, may legitimately employ force in the administration of justice.

2. The Moral Insufficiency of Retribution

Retribution—punishment motivated by a desire for revenge—fails on several moral grounds:

  1. Moral Symmetry: If the former regime used violence to oppress, responding with violence replicates its tactics. The moral critique of the dictatorship must be reflected in the means employed to confront it; otherwise, the new order becomes indistinguishable from the old.

  2. Proportionality and Desert: Even if one accepts a desert‑based theory of punishment, the determination of desert requires impartial institutions, not individual judgments. Private actors lack the capacity to assess guilt, assign proportional punishment, or ensure due process.

  3. The Principle of Non‑Instrumentalization: Kantian ethics forbids treating persons merely as means to an end. Using an ex‑oppressor as a vehicle for one’s own catharsis instrumentalizes them, violating respect for their intrinsic dignity.

Thus, retribution alone cannot generate a moral right to violence; it must be embedded within a broader framework of justice that respects the rule of law and human dignity.

3. Practical Risks of Private Violence

Beyond moral philosophy, historical experience demonstrates the destabilising consequences of vigilante justice in post‑dictatorial societies:

  • Cycle of Revenge: Violence begets violence. In the immediate aftermath of regimes such as Franco’s Spain or the military junta in Argentina, sporadic acts of retaliation triggered retaliatory attacks, threatening the fragile peace.
  • Undermining Institutions: When individuals take the law into their own hands, they erode public confidence in emerging courts and transitional mechanisms. This weakens the very institutions needed to guarantee long‑term accountability.
  • Selective Justice: Private actors are prone to bias—targeting not only genuine perpetrators but also their relatives, acquaintances, or political rivals. This leads to injustice and deepens societal divisions.

Empirical studies of transitional societies (e.g., South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, post‑communist Czechoslovakia) consistently show that societies that channel justice through formal, non‑violent mechanisms recover more sustainably than those that tolerate or encourage extrajudicial violence.

4. Alternatives to Retributive Violence

The failure of retribution does not imply impunity. Contemporary transitional justice offers a rich repertoire of non‑violent remedies:

  • Criminal Prosecutions: Where evidence exists, state‑run trials (domestic or international) can hold perpetrators accountable while upholding due‑process rights.
  • Truth Commissions: By documenting abuses, these bodies provide a public record, acknowledge victims, and foster collective healing without resort to vengeance.
  • Reparations and Memorialisation: Financial compensation, official apologies, and the preservation of memory serve both restorative and symbolic purposes.
  • Institutional Reform: Dismantling repressive agencies, vetting security forces, and establishing independent judiciaries prevent the recurrence of oppression.

These mechanisms aim at restorative rather than merely retributive goals, emphasising reconciliation, societal reconstruction, and the prevention of future harm.

5. The Philosophical Case for Restraint

Even from a just‑war perspective, violence can only be justified under strict conditions: legitimate authority, just cause, right intention, probability of success, and last resort. In a post‑dictatorial context, individuals lack legitimate authority; the “just cause” of ending oppression has already been achieved by the regime’s collapse; and non‑violent alternatives remain available, satisfying the criterion of last resort. Hence, the philosophical framework that governs the use of force decisively bars private violent retribution.

Moreover, a commitment to non‑violence signals a moral break with the dictatorship’s methods. It demonstrates that the new polity is capable of governing through law, not fear. This symbolic dimension is crucial for building a democratic culture where power is contested through institutions rather than through arms.

Conclusion

In the aftermath of a dictatorship, the desire for revenge is understandable—perhaps even natural. Yet moral philosophy, political theory, and the lessons of history converge on a clear conclusion: individuals do not possess a right to employ violence as a means of retributive justice after a regime’s fall. Retribution, standing alone, fails to meet the requirements of legitimate authority, proportionality, and respect for human dignity, and it threatens to plunge societies back into the cycles of terror they have just escaped.

A just transition requires that the monopoly on force be vested in democratic institutions, that accountability be pursued through transparent legal processes, and that societies embrace restorative approaches that acknowledge suffering without replicating it. Only by rejecting the false promise of vigilante vengeance can a post‑dictatorial polity lay the foundations for genuine, lasting peace.

Allowing or endorsing personal vengeance fractures communities further, creating new cycles of resentment and retaliation. Furthermore, retributive violence distracts from systemic reform. The goal after dictatorship should not merely be to punish individuals, but to dismantle the machinery of oppression and prevent its return. The fall of a dictatorship is a moment of profound rupture. The air is thick with a volatile mixture of relief, grief, and a burning, ancient hunger for justice. For those who lived under the boot of state terror, who lost loved ones to midnight raids and unmarked graves, the impulse to seek violent retribution against former oppressors is not only understandable—it feels morally righteous. Yet, while the anger is justified, the weaponization of that anger through personal or mob violence is a profound mistake. It corrupts the very idea of justice it claims to serve and sets the fragile new society on a path back to the tyranny it just escaped.

The argument against a right to violent retribution rests not on a denial of the victims' pain, but on a higher commitment to the principles that separate justice from vengeance. First, violence by individuals or groups is inherently subjective and chaotic. It operates on perception, rumor, and raw emotion, not on evidence or proportional guilt. A former low-level informant, coerced under threat to their family, might be lynched alongside a torturer who reveled in cruelty. This indiscriminate nature replaces the rule of law with the rule of the mob, creating a new cycle of victimization and terror. It sacrifices truth on the altar of immediate, visceral satisfaction.

Furthermore, retribution alone is a morally insufficient cause for violence. A society emerging from darkness must ask a more profound question than "How do we punish?" It must ask, "What do we want to become?" If the new order is built on the same foundational principle of extra-judicial killing as the old regime, it has merely changed the cast of characters, not the script. True justice seeks to restore moral balance, to affirm the value of the victims, and to rebuild a social contract based on dignity and law. Retributive violence achieves the opposite: it enshrines a hierarchy of suffering, validates the use of force as the ultimate arbiter of disputes, and poisons the well for reconciliation. It tells the next generation that power, not principle, is what matters.

History offers a clear warning. The "Reign of Terror" following the French Revolution saw the revolutionaries, having toppled the monarchy, begin to devour their own through the guillotine, in a paranoid spiral that killed thousands and ultimately paved the way for Napoleon's authoritarian rule. Conversely, the path of South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), while imperfect and deeply painful, chose a different route. It prioritized public testimony, acknowledgment of crimes, and conditional amnesty over widespread retributive violence. This did not satisfy every survivor's desire for punishment, but it forged a national narrative of "never again," allowing the new democracy to be built on a foundation of documented truth rather than buried resentment and unending blood feuds.

This is not a call for impunity. It is a demand for superior justice. The energy of righteous anger must be channeled not into the private sword, but into the public forge of legitimate institutions. This means:

  1. Truth-Seeking: Establishing official, transparent processes to document crimes, name the dead, and give survivors a voice.
  2. Formal Accountability: Creating specialized courts, whether domestic or international, to try the architects of oppression based on evidence and due process, however imperfect.
  3. Structural Reform: Dismantling the systems of oppression—purging security services, rewriting constitutions, and guaranteeing civil liberties—to ensure the regime cannot return in another form.

The claim of a "right" to violent retribution is ultimately a claim that individuals or groups can supersede the collective, democratic project of building a just state. It is a recipe for perpetual conflict, where today's avengers become tomorrow's targets. The hardest, most courageous path is to reject the seductive logic of the vendetta. It requires victims and the new polity to wield a power greater than that of their former oppressors: the power to build a system where guilt is determined by facts, punishment is administered without hatred, and the ultimate goal is not the satisfaction of revenge, but the construction of a lasting peace.

Justice must be a light that illuminates the path forward, not a torch that burns down the house we all must now share.

An essential test of any society emerging from the long shadow of dictatorship is whether it can distinguish justice from vengeance. When oppression has ended, the impulse to punish those who wielded power cruelly is understandable and even emotionally vindicating. This essay will argue that retribution alone—however visceral or justified it may feel—cannot serve as a legitimate cause for violence, and that genuine justice must be sought through lawful and nonviolent means.

  1. The Rule of Law versus Vigilantism
    A central pillar of democratic governance is that no one person or faction holds the right to decide guilt and administer punishment on their own terms. If victims of a dictatorship resort to violence, they cease to be defenders of justice and instead become vigilantes. Such extrajudicial action bypasses fair trial guarantees, reliable evidence standards, and proportional sentencing. It transforms accountability into personal revenge and breeds uncertainty: when one group claims the moral high ground to use force, others will too. A stable transition demands institutions—courts, truth commissions, parliamentary inquiries—empowered to investigate, prosecute, and, when warranted, punish former wrongdoers within a transparent framework.

  2. The Perils of Collective Punishment
    Violence directed at former oppressors often spills over into reprisals against innocents or those only tangentially connected to the old regime. Family members, low‑level functionaries, even neutral citizens can become targets when personal vendettas masquerade as righteous warfare. Such indiscriminate or disproportionate violence exacerbates communal divisions and vandalizes the moral integrity of the new order. By contrast, measured legal processes distinguish between degrees of responsibility, preserve individual dignity, and protect the rights of the accused. In this way a society rebuilds on principles of fairness rather than raw passion.

  3. Breaking the Cycle of Violence
    Dictatorship itself is an extreme form of violence. Answering violence with more violence risks entrenching a never‑ending cycle: today’s avengers become tomorrow’s oppressors. History shows that societies which rise above the logic of “an eye for an eye” are better positioned to heal and transform. South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission, for example, strove to replace retaliation with frank testimony, public acknowledgment of wrongdoing, and—in certain cases—conditional amnesties. While no approach is perfect, it illustrates how restorative methods can secure both accountability and social cohesion more effectively than street reprisals or private militias.

  4. Upholding Universal Human Rights
    Respect for human rights cannot be suspended simply because the targets are former tyrants or collaborators. If the new society claims to champion the inviolability of human dignity, it must extend those protections neutrally, even to those once responsible for egregious abuses. To do otherwise is to assert that human rights are conditional—granted only to the favored—undermining the very concept of universal entitlement. By contrast, a rights‑based approach insists that due process, humane treatment, and proportionality apply without exception. This universalism strengthens the fledgling democracy’s moral credibility both at home and abroad.

  5. Psychological and Moral Renewal
    Retributive violence may offer individuals a fleeting sense of empowerment or catharsis, but it does little to confront the deeper traumas and resentments inflicted by dictatorships. Meaningful healing requires truth‑telling, communal acknowledgement of suffering, and constructive programs of rehabilitation for both victims and former perpetrators. These processes help societies to remember without becoming prisoners of rage. By resisting the urge to resort to private violence, citizens affirm their own humanity and set a higher standard for public life.

Conclusion
The moment a dictatorship falls is fraught with possibility—but also peril. While the desire for swift, personal vengeance against those who once oppressed us is powerful, it must not be permitted to override the principles of justice on which a free society will stand or fall. Retribution alone, without the checks and balances of law, due process, and respect for human rights, is a recipe for further turmoil and injustice. True justice demands patience, courage, and a commitment to nonviolent channels: courts that apply the rule of law, truth commissions that unearth facts, and dialogue that seeks reconciliation over retaliation. Only in this way can a nation not merely escape tyranny, but build a lasting peace grounded in fairness and respect for every individual’s dignity.

The primary argument against legitimizing violence for retribution lies in its inherent rejection of principled justice. Justice, to be meaningful and sustainable, must be rooted in established principles: due process, impartiality, proportionality, and accountability. Extrajudicial violence, perpetrated by individuals against former oppressors, bypasses these fundamental tenets. It replaces the careful weighing of evidence and application of law with the raw, subjective emotion of vengeance. While the desire for payback is visceral, vengeance is not justice. Vengeance is often indiscriminate, disproportionate, and driven by personal rage rather than a commitment to societal norms. Allowing individuals to act as judge, jury, and executioner based solely on their personal sense of grievance erodes the very concept of a fair and ordered system of justice. It replaces the rule of law with the rule of the mob or the individual avenger, undermining the potential for a stable, rights-respecting society emerging from the ashes of dictatorship.

Furthermore, resorting to violence for retribution carries immense practical and societal dangers. Transition periods after authoritarian collapse are inherently fragile. Societies are fractured, institutions are weak, and trust is eroded. Widespread vigilante violence or targeted assassinations destabilize the nascent order. They create an atmosphere of fear and insecurity that can easily be exploited by remnants of the old regime or other destabilizing forces. Such violence can reignite conflict, fracture communities further along personal or political lines, and provide propaganda fodder for those seeking to discredit the entire transition process. Crucially, it risks creating new victims and new grievances, perpetuating the cycle of violence the society sought to escape. The practical consequence of "justice" through violence is often more violence, hindering reconciliation and reconstruction rather than fostering them.

Advocates of retributive violence might argue that legal processes are too slow, too corrupt, or incapable of delivering meaningful accountability, especially if the new regime is weak or compromised. This is a legitimate concern. However, the solution is not to abandon justice altogether, but to demand and build better systems. The answer to past injustice should be strengthening the rule of law, supporting independent judiciaries, establishing robust truth and reconciliation commissions, and ensuring fair trials. While imperfect, these mechanisms offer a path towards accountability that is transparent, verifiable, and ultimately more legitimate than violent acts driven by personal vendetta. Societal healing requires acknowledging suffering collectively and through established processes, not through fragmented, potentially erroneous acts of individual violence. Mechanisms like South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission demonstrate how difficult truths can be aired, responsibility can be acknowledged (even without traditional punishment), and a foundation for future reconciliation can be laid – a path unavailable through vengeance.

Finally, it is essential to recognize that retribution alone is morally insufficient. While holding perpetrators accountable is crucial, justice encompasses more than punishment. It involves restoring dignity, acknowledging victims, repairing societal harm, and preventing future abuses. Violence, even against a former oppressor, often inflicts further trauma and fails to address these broader needs. It may provide a fleeting sense of satisfaction but rarely delivers genuine closure or healing for the victim or society. True justice seeks to build a future where such atrocities cannot recur, focusing on prevention and reconciliation, not just inflicting pain on those who caused it. Retribution fixates on the past wrong; justice must also look towards building a better future.

In conclusion, the understandable and powerful human impulse for retribution after the fall of a dictatorship cannot be allowed to sanctify extrajudicial violence. Retribution, standing alone, is an inadequate moral and practical justification for individuals to take the law into their own hands and inflict violence upon former oppressors. Such acts undermine the foundational principles of justice, destabilize fragile transitions, risk perpetuating cycles of violence, and fail to deliver the comprehensive healing and restoration that societies need. The path forward is challenging, demanding immense courage to build functional legal systems and pursue accountability through lawful, transparent, and principled means. It requires rejecting the seductive simplicity of vengeance in favor of the harder, but ultimately more just and sustainable, work of building a society grounded in the rule of law and the pursuit of genuine, restorative justice. Only then can a society truly break free from the shadows of its oppressive past.

Yet however understandable that impulse may be, individuals do not have a right to use violence to seek justice against former oppressors after a dictatorship falls. Retribution alone is not a sufficient cause for violence, because justice must be governed by law, equal moral principles, and the long-term needs of a society emerging from tyranny.

The most basic reason is that justice and vengeance are not the same thing. Justice aims to determine responsibility fairly, to impose proportionate consequences, and to uphold moral standards that apply to everyone. Vengeance, by contrast, is driven primarily by anger, pain, and the desire to make another suffer. After dictatorship, these emotions are powerful and often justified. But if individuals act on them through violence, they replace one form of arbitrary force with another. The central evil of dictatorship is not only that terrible acts were committed, but that power was exercised without restraint, accountability, or due process. If citizens answer that history with private violence, they risk reproducing the very logic of the regime they oppose: that might, passion, and opportunity are enough to determine who lives, who suffers, and who dies.

A right to use violence cannot rest on the mere fact that someone deserves punishment. Many people may deserve punishment in a moral sense, but punishment in a lawful society must be imposed through institutions, evidence, and procedures. This is especially important after a dictatorship, when facts are often contested, records are incomplete, and responsibility may vary widely. Some officials were architects of oppression; others were minor participants; some acted under coercion; some are falsely accused. Individual retaliation ignores these distinctions. It treats suspicion as proof and rage as judgment. That is why retribution alone is not a sufficient cause for violence: desert does not automatically authorize private force. To claim otherwise is to grant each injured person the authority to serve as investigator, judge, and executioner.

Moreover, private violence after regime change threatens the possibility of rebuilding a political community based on rights. A society emerging from dictatorship must establish trust in public institutions, the rule of law, and common standards of accountability. If people begin settling scores through beatings, assassinations, or mob attacks, the transition can quickly descend into cycles of retaliation. Former oppressors may strike back, their allies may organize in defense, and old divisions may harden into new conflicts. Instead of a clean break from authoritarianism, the society inherits a culture in which violence remains a normal instrument of politics. That outcome betrays victims rather than honoring them, because it prevents the emergence of a stable order in which abuses can actually be prevented from recurring.

There is also a deeper moral principle at stake: human rights do not depend on innocence. Even wrongdoers possess basic rights not to be tortured, maimed, or killed outside legitimate legal necessity. To deny this is to make rights conditional on virtue, which destroys their universality. The purpose of rights is precisely to restrain what people may do even to those they hate and even to those who have acted monstrously. If former oppressors can be attacked by private individuals simply because they deserve it, then rights become little more than privileges temporarily enjoyed by the powerful or the popular. A post-dictatorial society must reject that view if it hopes to become genuinely just.

Some may object that legal institutions after dictatorship are often weak, compromised, or unavailable. Courts may be corrupt, police may include former regime loyalists, and official justice may be delayed or denied. These are serious realities. But the failure of institutions does not create a general individual right to violent retribution. At most, it underscores the urgency of building credible mechanisms of accountability, such as trials, truth commissions, lustration policies, reparations, and international prosecutions where necessary. It may also justify limited defensive violence in situations of immediate threat. If a former torturer is actively attacking someone, force may be used in self-defense. But that is different from retaliatory violence aimed at punishing past wrongs. Self-defense prevents imminent harm; retribution answers completed harm with new harm. The former may be justified by necessity, while the latter cannot be justified merely by anger or moral desert.

In fact, insisting that individuals lack a right to violent revenge does not mean asking victims to forget or forgive. Memory, condemnation, and punishment are all compatible with rejecting private violence. A society can honor victims by exposing the truth, preserving testimony, prosecuting perpetrators, removing them from positions of power, compensating survivors, and publicly repudiating the old regime. It may gratify those who inflict it, but it often obscures truth, eliminates opportunities for testimony, creates martyrs, and weakens legal norms. It may feel like justice in the moment, yet leave a society more fragmented and less capable of confronting its past honestly. Retribution is a powerful human impulse, but moral and political legitimacy require more than impulse.

For these reasons, individuals do not have a right to use violence to seek justice against former oppressors after a dictatorship falls. The suffering caused by tyranny may explain the desire for revenge, but it does not transform revenge into a right. If post-dictatorial justice is to mean anything, it must reject arbitrary violence even when directed at the guilty. Retribution alone is not a sufficient cause for violence, because true justice depends on law, restraint, and a commitment to human dignity that survives even the worst abuses of history.

When a dictatorship collapses, the wounds it leaves behind are deep: torture chambers, mass graves, stolen years, shattered families, and the lasting humiliation of being systematically dehumanized. In such a context, it is understandable that some people feel an overwhelming urge to strike back at those who brutalized them. Yet understanding that impulse is not the same as validating it. Individuals do not have a right to use violence to seek justice against their former oppressors, and retribution alone is not a sufficient cause for violence. To accept such a right is to undermine accountability, erode the moral basis of the new order, and jeopardize the very possibility of genuine justice and lasting peace.

First, allowing individuals to claim a right to violent retribution after a dictatorship falls destroys the distinction between justice and vengeance. Justice is backward-looking in that it addresses past wrongs, but it is also principled: it is constrained by rules, evidence, proportionality, and respect for human rights, even when directed against those who once violated them. Vengeance is driven by emotion and injury, unconstrained by impartial standards and focused less on upholding a norm than on inflicting suffering. If individuals may justly attack former oppressors simply because those oppressors “deserve it,” then the measure of what is permitted becomes subjective anger rather than universal principle.

This collapse has serious consequences. Once the moral prohibition on private violence is relaxed for one group, others will claim the same license: collaborators, suspected informants, members of the old ruling ethnic, religious, or political group. Old grievances and new suspicions quickly expand the circle of “legitimate” targets beyond those directly and demonstrably responsible for atrocities. The result is not justice, but a widening spiral of arbitrary harm. A system that aims to break with dictatorship must be built on impartial standards precisely to avoid reproducing the dictatorship’s own logic—where power and grievance, not law, decide who may be harmed.

Second, the idea of a “right” to retaliatory violence contradicts the core principles that make justice meaningful after oppression. If the new society is to be morally superior to the regime it replaces, it cannot adopt the regime’s most fundamental premise: that human beings may be deliberately harmed outside a framework that respects their inherent dignity. Rights are not tests of moral worth. They are shields that apply even to those who have done wrong—shields that limit how we punish, not whether we may hold them accountable at all. When we deny former oppressors the protection of law and due process and subject them to individual violence, we affirm that rights are conditional on behavior or identity; this is the same reasoning that tyrants employ.

To enforce accountability through legal institutions is not to “go easy” on perpetrators; it is to insist that punishment itself must be governed by principles. Trials, evidence, opportunity for defense, proportionate sentencing—these disciplines do more than safeguard the accused. They protect the integrity of the new order and signal that, unlike the dictatorship, it will not sacrifice human dignity to rage or expediency. A right to private vengeance would invert that signal. It tells victims that their suffering entitles them to suspend the very norms whose violation they rightly condemned. This risks moral incoherence: if torture, extrajudicial killing, and degradation were wrong when inflicted by the regime, they do not become right when inflicted on its agents by individuals, no matter how understandable the anger.

Third, retributive violence by individuals undermines the rule of law at the very moment when it must be strengthened. The end of a dictatorship leaves a vacuum: institutions are fragile, trust is brittle, and political competition is tense. In that environment, legitimizing private violence, even against those widely regarded as guilty, sends a dangerous message: violence is an acceptable instrument of political and moral judgment. That message is easily exploited. Factions can disguise vendettas and power grabs as “people’s justice.” Political rivals can be branded former collaborators and eliminated. Resentment between groups hardens into cycles of reprisal that make democratic consolidation far more difficult.

By contrast, insisting that only lawful, collectively authorized channels may pursue wrongdoers is not a technicality; it is an act of reconstruction. It encourages individuals to transfer their claims from personal retaliation to public institutions. It binds the new government to take those claims seriously—through trials, truth commissions, reparations, and lustration—without conceding that anyone may unilaterally decide who deserves harm. The discipline of law is precisely what prevents accountability from degenerating into collective punishment of entire communities associated with the old regime, which would perpetuate divisions and plant the seeds of future violence.

Fourth, the insufficiency of retribution alone as a justification for violence becomes clearer once we distinguish between legitimate punishment and morally corrosive cruelty. Retributive justice, in its defensible form, holds that wrongdoing warrants proportionate sanction: the perpetrator should be held responsible, and the response should affirm the violated norm. However, even in that framework, several constraints apply:

  • Guilt must be individuated, not assumed by association.
  • The response must be proportionate, not excessive or degrading.
  • The process must be reliable, not driven by rumor or passion.
  • The sanction must be imposed by a legitimate authority, not by whoever is strong enough or angry enough.

Private violence in the aftermath of dictatorship systematically violates these constraints. It cannot reliably distinguish levels of responsibility, rarely respects proportionality, is prone to misidentification, and accumulates symbolic and physical excess. Even when directed at genuine perpetrators, it seeks satisfaction rather than the careful affirmation of norms. The mere fact that someone did terrible things does not license anyone else to do terrible things to them. The moral intuition that “they deserve to suffer” cannot, by itself, override the need to preserve humane limits on our own conduct.

Nor does violent revenge succeed at what it promises emotionally. It does not restore the dead, heal trauma, or erase humiliation. It often leaves victims’ families entangled in new forms of violence, legal risk, and moral unease. It can trap societies in narratives of perpetual retaliation, where each new act of harm is framed as a justified answer to the last. The desire for retribution is real; but to convert that desire into a right to violence is to mistake a psychological impulse for a moral principle.

Fifth, refusing a right to private violent retribution opens space for more constructive forms of justice that still take the gravity of past crimes seriously. After a dictatorship, societies are not faced with a binary choice between vengeance and impunity. They can pursue:

  • Criminal prosecutions of those most responsible, including former leaders, commanders, and direct perpetrators of gross abuses.
  • Truth commissions that document what happened, recognize victims, and break the silence that allowed impunity.
  • Institutional reforms and vetting, excluding from positions of power those who participated in systemic abuses.
  • Reparations and memorialization, which acknowledge harm and affirm the equal worth of victims.

These mechanisms are imperfect, frequently too slow or incomplete, and often painful. But they have one crucial advantage: they respect the principle that no one—victims included—may unilaterally place others outside the protection of law. They balance the demands of accountability with the demands of stability and reconciliation. They also protect the moral standing of victims and resisters, who can claim that they did not become what they fought against.

The refusal to endorse individual violence against former oppressors is thus not a betrayal of victims; it is a defense of their deepest claim—that what was done to them was objectively wrong because human beings must never be treated as disposable instruments. To say that a former torturer cannot be lynched in the street is not to minimize his crimes; it is to insist that even for him, the community will not abandon the principles that give its condemnation weight.

In sum, individuals do not have a right to use violence to seek justice against former oppressors after a dictatorship falls, because such a right would:

  • Erase the line between justice and vengeance.
  • Undermine the universality of rights and mimic the logic of tyranny.
  • Corrode the rule of law at a critical moment of political reconstruction.
  • Fail the moral tests of proportionality, reliability, and legitimate authority.
  • Obstruct more principled paths to accountability and reconciliation.

Retribution as raw payback is, on its own, an insufficient ground for violence. The challenge for societies emerging from dictatorship is not to deny the longing for redress, but to transform it—to channel anger and grief into lawful, principled mechanisms that punish genuine wrongdoers, recognize victims, and lay a foundation on which a just political community can stand.

The fall of a dictatorship is a moment of cathartic liberation, often accompanied by a torrent of suppressed rage and a profound desire for vengeance.
